beats.t: It's forty degrees in the desert, and this guy is eating a bowl of ice. Long before refrigerators existed.
So where did the ice come from? This giant dome.
It's called a yakhchal, which literally means ice pit.
It all starts in winter. Water from an underground channel is led into long, shallow pools next to the dome.
Right beside the pools, they build a huge wall, so the pools stay in the shade all day long.
On clear winter nights, the desert gets freezing cold, and the shallow water turns to ice.
Every morning, workers break the ice into blocks and carry it inside the dome.
Down into a deep pit, where it's stacked up and packed with straw.
Now here's the clever part. The walls of the dome are up to two meters thick at the bottom.
They're made of a special mortar called sarooj. Sand, clay, lime, ash, and even goat hair and egg whites.
It blocks the heat so well that the ice inside barely melts.
And the tall cone shape lets hot air rise out through the top, while the cold air sinks down to the ice.
Any ice that does melt drains away through a trench at the bottom, so the rest stays dry and frozen.
So by the middle of summer, there's still ice. Enough for the whole town.
Some of these domes are still standing in Iran today, hundreds of years later.
All of that with no electricity. Just shade, cold nights, and really thick walls.
